description: Just two people interested in space.
summary: LunaLink is an interactive platform for direct comparison of Lunar and Earth sites. The platform provides tools for extracting and computing data from open-source platforms covering both the Earth and the Moon. The aim of the project is to provide a coherent tool for collecting the highest amount of usable data available for a user-selected Lunar site, which is then used to scan the whole of the Earth to determine places, which are of high similarity based on the specified parameters (also user-defined). The platform distinguishes between two main fields for comparison - site topography and light/thermal conditions with no mixing between them and overall scoring. For topography more than 20 different parameters are extracted from raw data and then converted into 5 different categories for similarity scoring, including terrain relief (3D maps when available), soil chemistry and ice abundance. The same approach is implemented for the illumination and thermal branch, which compares data from multiple sources to build detailed shadow, irradiance and thermal maps. These are then evaluated based on a weighted formula to give a percentage score of similarity for testing. The output presents a score for both fields along with the filtered raw data for detailed inspection and evaluation of testing conditions.
details:
What it does. LunaLink is a python based web comparator of locations on the Moon and the Earth. The websites has a home page which displays already computed results (from its own algorithms) for known 2 known Lunar sites and one arbitrarily chosen coordinate point, which showcase its capabilities. Besides that there are two evaluator pages - LTC (Light, Thermal, Combined) and TSI (Topography, Soil Chemistry, Ice). These two page have six comparator areas overall, which have different parameters used for estimating a similarity score between Lunar and Earth sites. The evaluators allow choosing of any point on the Moon as a center of the area of interest, for which then the significant data is extract from multiple sources and then the whole Earth is searched for best matches based on our scoring policies. Ones sites with relevant scores are detected and subsequently reported, the user can see the scoring results, but also the filtered raw data for both the Moon and Earth sites in a pop-up window, when clicking on the individual analog site's icon.

How it works. Every evaluator follows the same process: choose a lunar target, extract its conditions from source data, compare the same physical quantity on Earth, and score each difference against a stated tolerance (100 × exp(−(difference/tolerance)²)).

  • Light: models the Sun over a full year at 10-minute steps on both bodies (JPL DE421 via Skyfield; NOAA solar equations), comparing sun-elevation distributions, sunlit fraction and longest darkness, with optional terrain horizons from LOLA and ETOPO.
  • Thermal: pairs MODIS land-surface temperatures with LRO Diviner lunar temperatures at the same local solar time, then checks the shortlist against NASA POWER.
  • Combined: weights light and thermal 50/50 and requires both.
  • Topography: compares slope, relief and roughness of equal-radius circles (LOLA vs NOAA ETOPO 2022, about 2 km cells) for every prepared 1° Earth land centre, then optionally adds crater-like depression density and boulder density measured with a published Mask R-CNN boulder detector (BoulderNet) on LROC NAC and Earth aerial imagery.
  • Soil chemistry: compares Lunar Prospector oxide abundances with GloRiSe river-sediment analyses, requiring every oxide to pass its tolerance.
  • Hydrogen & Ice: compares Lunar Prospector hydrogen with Arctic frozen-ground samples converted to hydrogen proxies, and reports ice-condition evidence separately.

There is also a Lunar Surface Maps functionality, which is just a byproduct feature of the development process, but can be very useful for analyzing specifically the moon site of interest. It provides thermal, irradiance, shadows and terrain maps with the highest attainable resolution from open-source data.

To implement the features for every point on the Moon and Earth, the evaluators might fetch data in real time, so it might take some more time. Also 3D maps are known to take some time due to the volume of data.

What makes it trustworthy. Missing data are never treated as zero or as a match; combined scores are withheld when evidence is incomplete. Every result keeps its source, resolution, date and coverage, and can be exported as JSON. Scores are exploratory match indices, not probabilities or proof of suitability, and the tool says so.

Benefits. Mission planners and test engineers can choose Earth analog sites for a specific test objective (power, thermal, mobility, in-situ resource use) and see at once where an analog falls short. LunaLink is a robust and extensive tool that fuses every open-source data we could reach to find the best matches for Lunar missions testing on Earth, and does it in a simple an detailed fashion through a basic GUI.

Tools. Python 3.12 (NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Shapely, Skyfield, PyTorch/Detectron2), a static HTML/CSS/JavaScript front end with globe.gl, a single gateway serving four Python API services, and deployment as a Docker app on Hugging Face Spaces.
